item.question: Compare a 10 cm by 1 cm strip with a 5 cm by 4 cm rectangle: perimeter and area.
steps: Strip perimeter: 2 × (10 + 1) = 22 cm. Strip area: 10 × 1 = 10 cm².
Rectangle perimeter: 2 × (5 + 4) = 18 cm. Rectangle area: 5 × 4 = 20 cm².
item.answer: The strip has the larger perimeter (22 cm) but the smaller area (10 cm²)
item.text:
Worked example: Compare a 10 cm by 1 cm strip with a 5 cm by 4 cm rectangle: perimeter and area.
1. Strip perimeter: 2 × (10 + 1) = 22 cm. Strip area: 10 × 1 = 10 cm².
2. Rectangle perimeter: 2 × (5 + 4) = 18 cm. Rectangle area: 5 × 4 = 20 cm².
3. 22 > 18 but 10 < 20.
Answer: The strip has the larger perimeter (22 cm) but the smaller area (10 cm²)

item.question: Compare a 4 by 4 square with a thin zigzag made of 9 unit squares joined edge to edge in one line with bends.
steps: Square: perimeter 4 × 4 = 16 units, area 16 square units.
Zigzag: each square shares edges with its neighbours, leaving 2 × 9 + 2 = 20 unit edges on the boundary, so perimeter 20 units.
Zigzag area: 9 square units.
item.answer: The zigzag has the larger perimeter (20 units against 16) but the smaller area (9 against 16)

item.question: Identify the missing sidelengths. (i) A plus shaped figure is made of four rectangles: a 28 in² piece whose right edge rises 4 in above a 21 in² piece of length 7 in, a 35 in² piece of width 3 in plus the width of the 28 in² piece, and a 14 in² strip that hangs 2 in below the 35 in² piece; find the width of the 14 in² strip. (ii) A 29 m² piece and an 11 m² piece are both 4 m tall, and the bold rectangle made of the 29 m² piece and the piece below it has area 50 m²; find the missing sides.
steps_tex: (i): The $21$ in$^2$ piece is $7$ in long, so its height is $21 \div 7 = 3$ in.
The $28$ in$^2$ piece is $4 + 3 = 7$ in tall, so its width is $28 \div 7 = 4$ in.
The $35$ in$^2$ piece is $3 + 4 = 7$ in wide, so its height is $35 \div 7 = 5$ in.
The $14$ in$^2$ strip is $5 + 2 = 7$ in tall, so its width is $14 \div 7 = 2$ in.
The lower piece has area $50 - 29 = 21\text{ m}^2$ and width $7.25\text{ m}$, so its height is $21 \div 7.25 \approx 2.9\text{ m}$.
item.answer_tex: (i): $2$ in, with $3$ in, $4$ in and $5$ in on the way. (ii): $7.25\text{ m}$ and $2.75\text{ m}$ across the top, and a lower height of $\frac{84}{29}\text{ m}$, about $2.9\text{ m}$
steps: (i) The 21 in² piece is 7 in long, so its height is 21 ÷ 7 = 3 in.
The 28 in² piece is 4 + 3 = 7 in tall, so its width is 28 ÷ 7 = 4 in.
The 35 in² piece is 3 + 4 = 7 in wide, so its height is 35 ÷ 7 = 5 in.
The 14 in² strip is 5 + 2 = 7 in tall, so its width is 14 ÷ 7 = 2 in.
(ii) Top widths: 29 ÷ 4 = 7.25 m and 11 ÷ 4 = 2.75 m.
The lower piece has area 50 − 29 = 21 m² and width 7.25 m, so its height is 21 ÷ 7.25 ≈ 2.9 m.
item.answer: (i) 2 in, with 3 in, 4 in and 5 in on the way. (ii) 7.25 m and 2.75 m across the top, and a lower height of 84/29 m, about 2.9 m
item.text:
$1$. (i): The $21$ in$^2$ piece is $7$ in long, so its height is $21 \div 7 = 3$ in.
$2$. The $28$ in$^2$ piece is $4 + 3 = 7$ in tall, so its width is $28 \div 7 = 4$ in.
$3$. The $35$ in$^2$ piece is $3 + 4 = 7$ in wide, so its height is $35 \div 7 = 5$ in.
$4$. The $14$ in$^2$ strip is $5 + 2 = 7$ in tall, so its width is $14 \div 7 = 2$ in.
$5$. (ii): Top widths: $29 \div 4 = 7.25\text{ m}$ and $11 \div 4 = 2.75\text{ m}$.
$6$. The lower piece has area $50 - 29 = 21\text{ m}^2$ and width $7.25\text{ m}$, so its height is $21 \div 7.25 \approx 2.9\text{ m}$.
Answer: (i): $2$ in, with $3$ in, $4$ in and $5$ in on the way. (ii): $7.25\text{ m}$ and $2.75\text{ m}$ across the top, and a lower height of $\frac{84}{29}\text{ m}$, about $2.9\text{ m}$
item.s_figure: Figure (i) with the unknown sides found as 3 in, 4 in, 5 in and 2 in, and figure (ii) with the top widths 7.25 m and 2.75 m and the lower height of about 2.9 m marked.

video.title: How do we find the area of a path around a park?
video.description: A path is laid around a rectangular park, and the park and the path together make a bigger rectangle. The area of the park is taken away from the area of the bigger rectangle, and the answer is checked by cutting the path into four strips.

maths_rules: chosen values: outer rectangle ABCD 20 m by 14 m, park EFGH 16 m by 10 m
area of ABCD = 20 × 14 = 280 m²; area of EFGH = 16 × 10 = 160 m²
area of path = 280 − 160 = 120 m²; formula: area of ABCD − area of EFGH
moving ABCD with the park kept inside: both rectangles keep their sizes, so the path area stays 120 m²
check: path 2 m wide on every side ((20 − 16) ÷ 2 = 2 and (14 − 10) ÷ 2 = 2); two strips 20 × 2 = 40 each, two strips 10 × 2 = 20 each; 2 × 40 + 2 × 20 = 80 + 40 = 120 m²

item.question: A path (the shaded portion) is laid around a rectangular park EFGH inside a rectangle ABCD. (i) What measurements do you need to find the area of the path? Assign values and give a formula. (ii) If the width of the path along each side is given, can you find its area? If not, what else do you need? (iii) Does the area of the path change when the outer rectangle is moved while keeping the park inside it?
steps: (i) Measure the length and width of ABCD and of EFGH.
Area of path = area of ABCD − area of EFGH. With ABCD 20 m by 14 m and EFGH 16 m by 10 m: 20 × 14 − 16 × 10 = 280 − 160 = 120 m².

(ii) The widths alone are not enough; we also need the park's length and width. With a park 16 m by 10 m and widths 2 m on every side, break the path into two long strips 20 m by 2 m and two short strips 10 m by 2 m: 2 × 40 + 2 × 20 = 120 m².
(iii) Moving ABCD around the park changes the widths but not the two rectangles, so the path area stays the same.
item.answer: (i) Path area = area of ABCD − area of EFGH (120 m² for the chosen values). (ii) Also need the park's sides; same 120 m². (iii) No, the area does not change
item.text:
Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 2): A path (the shaded portion) is laid around a rectangular park EFGH inside a rectangle ABCD. (i) What measurements do you need to find the area of the path? Assign values and give a formula. (ii) If the width of the path along each side is given, can you find its area? If not, what else do you need? (iii) Does the area of the path change when the outer rectangle is moved while keeping the park inside it?
1. (i) Measure the length and width of ABCD and of EFGH.
2. Area of path = area of ABCD − area of EFGH. With ABCD 20 m by 14 m and EFGH 16 m by 10 m: 20 × 14 − 16 × 10 = 280 − 160 = 120 m².
3. (ii) The widths alone are not enough; we also need the park's length and width. With a park 16 m by 10 m and widths 2 m on every side, break the path into two long strips 20 m by 2 m and two short strips 10 m by 2 m: 2 × 40 + 2 × 20 = 120 m².
4. (iii) Moving ABCD around the park changes the widths but not the two rectangles, so the path area stays the same.
Answer: (i) Path area = area of ABCD − area of EFGH (120 m² for the chosen values). (ii) Also need the park's sides; same 120 m². (iii) No, the area does not change

item.text:
Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 3): A plot has sides 14 m and 12 m with a crosspath. What other measurements do you need to find the area of the crosspath? Assign values and give a formula.
1. We need the widths of the two paths: p for the path along the 14 m side and q for the path along the 12 m side.
2. The two strips are 14 × p and 12 × q, but they overlap in a p by q square counted twice.
3. Area = 14p + 12q − pq. With p = 1 m and q = 2 m: 14 × 1 + 12 × 2 − 1 × 2 = 14 + 24 − 2 = 36 m².
Answer: The widths of the two paths; area = 14p + 12q − pq, which is 36 m² when the widths are 1 m and 2 m

item.question: Find the area of the spiral tube shown in the figure. The tube has the same width (1 unit) throughout, and its straight parts measure 20, 20, 20, 15, 15, 10, 10, 5 and 5 along the outside.
steps: The hint: an L shaped tube with arms 5 and 5 has the same area as a straight tube of length 5 + 5 − 1 = 9, because the corner square is counted in both arms.
Add all the straight lengths: 20 + 20 + 20 + 15 + 15 + 10 + 10 + 5 + 5 = 120.
There are 8 bends, each counted twice, so subtract 8: 120 − 8 = 112.
The straightened tube is 112 units long and 1 unit wide: 112 × 1 = 112.

item.question: A triangle has base 8 cm and height 5 cm. Find its area.
steps: Its outer rectangle is 8 cm by 5 cm, area 8 × 5 = 40 cm².
The triangle is half of it.
item.text:
Worked example: A triangle has base 8 cm and height 5 cm. Find its area.
1. Its outer rectangle is 8 cm by 5 cm, area 8 × 5 = 40 cm².
2. The triangle is half of it.
3. Area = 1/2 × 8 × 5 = 20 cm².
Answer: 20 cm²

item.question: In an obtuse triangle ABC the height from A meets CB extended at D, with h = 4 cm, DB = 3 cm and BC = 6 cm. Find the area.
steps: DC = DB + BC = 3 + 6 = 9 cm.
Area of ΔADC = 1/2 × 4 × 9 = 18 cm². Area of ΔADB = 1/2 × 4 × 3 = 6 cm².
Area of ΔABC = 18 − 6 = 12 cm², and 1/2 × 4 × 6 = 12 cm² too.
item.answer: 12 cm², the same as 1/2 × base × height

video.title: How do we find the area of an isosceles triangle from half of it?

maths_rules: triangle SUB is isosceles with SU = SB; SE is perpendicular to UB; area of triangle SEB = 24 square units
in an isosceles triangle the perpendicular from the apex S meets UB at its midpoint, so UE = EB
triangles SUE and SEB have equal bases UE and EB and the same height SE, so equal areas: 1/2 × UE × SE = 1/2 × EB × SE = 24
area of triangle SUB = 24 + 24 = 48 square units
check: folding along SE puts triangle SUE exactly on triangle SEB, so SUB is double SEB: 2 × 24 = 48

video.title: How can we change a rectangle into a triangle of equal area?
video.description: The Shulba Sutras ask for a method to change a rectangle into a triangle with the same area. Extend the bottom side by its own length and join the new end to the top corner, and the triangle on the double base has the rectangle's area.

item.question: [Śulba-Sūtras] Give a method to transform a rectangle into a triangle of equal area.
steps: Take rectangle ABCD with base AB and height BC.
Extend AB to E so that BE = AB. Then AE is twice the base.
Join E to D. Triangle AED has base 2 × AB and height AD, so its area is 1/2 × 2AB × AD = AB × AD.
Another way: cut the rectangle along a diagonal and place the two halves side by side along the height to form one triangle.
item.answer: A triangle on double the base with the same height (or double the height on the same base) has the rectangle's area

video.title: How can we change a triangle into a rectangle of equal area?
video.description: The Shulba Sutras ask for a method to change a triangle into a rectangle with the same area. Join the middles of the two slanting sides, cut off the top triangle, cut it down its height, and turn its two halves down into the gaps. The result is a rectangle on the same base with half the height.
video.anchor: the triangle ABC of the book, with its height AX on the base BC
maths_rules: triangle ABC with height AX on base BC; M and N are the midpoints of AB and AC; MN is parallel to BC at half the height
cut off the top triangle AMN and cut it along the height from A to MN, which meets MN at T, into two right triangles AMT and ANT
turn triangle AMT half way round about M: A goes to B and T goes to a point directly above B at height 1/2 AX; turn ANT the same way about N
the lower part BCNM and the two turned triangles make a rectangle with base BC and height 1/2 AX
area = BC × 1/2 AX = 1/2 × BC × AX, the area of the triangle
check with base 8 and height 6: triangle 1/2 × 8 × 6 = 24; rectangle 8 × 3 = 24

final_answer.value: Join the midpoints of the two sides, cut off the top triangle, cut it along its height and turn the halves down: a rectangle on the same base with half the height
final_answer.spoken: join the middles of the two slanting sides, cut off the top triangle, cut it down its height and turn the halves down, to get a rectangle on the same base with half the height

item.question: [Śulba-Sūtras] Give a method to transform a triangle into a rectangle of equal area.
steps: Draw the height AX of triangle ABC on base BC.
Mark the midpoints of AB and AC and join them; this line is parallel to BC at half the height.
Drop perpendiculars from the two midpoints to BC. Cut off the two small top triangles and turn each into the gap below it.
The result is a rectangle with base BC and height 1/2 AX, so its area is 1/2 × BC × AX.
item.answer: Cut along the line joining the midpoints of the two sides and swing the top pieces down: a rectangle on the same base with half the height
